# Noam Chomsky: Concise Summary
Noam Chomsky, born in 1928 in Philadelphia to Ashkenazi Jewish immigrants, emerged as a pivotal figure in linguistics, philosophy, and political activism. He was educated at the University of Pennsylvania and Harvard, later joining MIT, where he founded the graduate program in linguistics. Chomsky revolutionized linguistics with his theory of generative grammar and biolinguistics, arguing that language is a biologically preset, species-specific cognitive structure. He introduced the concept of universal grammar, asserting that all humans share underlying linguistic structures, and his work catalyzed the "cognitive revolution" in linguistics and cognitive science. Chomsky’s contributions extended to formal language theory—the Chomsky hierarchy—and his critique of behaviorism fueled a major paradigm shift in psychology.
Politically, Chomsky is known for his steadfast libertarian socialist and anarcho-syndicalist views, consistently criticizing American imperialism, capitalism, and mainstream media manipulation through the "propaganda model" (as articulated in "Manufacturing Consent"). He has controversially defended freedom of speech, including for figures espousing Holocaust denial, which significantly affected his reputation, especially in France. Chomsky’s activism spans anti-war movements, critiques of U.S. foreign policy, support for East Timorese independence, and deep engagement with the Israeli–Palestinian conflict. Renowned as one of the most cited and influential intellectuals of his era, Chomsky’s copious academic and political writings have earned him numerous honors and have made him a landmark figure in global debates on language, cognition, media, and power. Despite recent health setbacks, he remains a symbol of critical dissent and intellectual rigor.
